label: Free Cinema
defn: The British documentary movement of 1956–1959 (Lindsay Anderson, Karel Reisz, Tony Richardson, Lorenza Mazzetti) whose six National Film Theatre programmes showed unscripted, personal films of working-class leisure and labour (O Dreamland, Every Day Except Christmas). Its directors went on to the British New Wave (A1-10).

label: Ukrainian Poetic Cinema
defn: The Kyiv (Dovzhenko Studio) school of the mid-1960s to late 1970s — Parajanov, Ilyenko, Osyka, Ivchenko, Mykolaichuk — making folkloric, painterly, ritual-saturated films of Ukrainian village and legend (Shadows of Forgotten Ancestors, The White Bird Marked with Black).

label: Korean New Wave
defn: The South Korean art cinema of c. 1987–1996 (Park Kwang-su, Jang Sun-woo, Lee Myung-se, Park Jong-won) that, after democratisation, turned realist and modernist means on division, labour and the Gwangju massacre (Chilsu and Mansu, A Petal, A Single Spark); it precedes the commercial Korean Wave of the 2000s.

label: Thai New Wave
defn: The revival of Thai cinema from 1997 by directors from advertising and music video — Pen-Ek Ratanaruang, Nonzee Nimibutr, Wisit Sasanatieng, the Pang brothers — mixing pastiche, colour stylisation and genre (Tears of the Black Tiger, 6ixtynin9, Monrak Transistor).

label: Nuevo Cine Mexicano
defn: The 1990s–2000s renewal of Mexican cinema (Arturo Ripstein's late films, María Novaro, Jorge Fons, Alfonso Cuarón, Alejandro González Iñárritu, Antonio Serrano) after the IMCINE reforms: urban, frank, internationally co-produced films (Danzón, Midaq Alley, Y tu mamá también).

label: Cinema of Transgression
defn: Nick Zedd's 1985 name for the New York Lower East Side Super-8 underground (Zedd, Richard Kern, Lydia Lunch, Tessa Hughes-Freeland) of deliberately shocking, punk, sexually and violently taboo films (Fingered, They Eat Scum).
see: A1-22 No Wave Cinema; A20-2 Underground Film

label: Fantaterror
defn: The Spanish horror boom of c. 1968–1980 — Paul Naschy's Waldemar Daninsky werewolf films, Amando de Ossorio's Blind Dead, Narciso Ibáñez Serrador, Vicente Aranda, León Klimovsky — mixing gothic monsters, Templar ghouls and late-Franco-era sexual and Catholic dread (Tombs of the Blind Dead, The House That Screamed).
secs: Amando de Ossorio & the Blind Dead

label: Ramsay Brothers Horror
defn: The Hindi low-budget horror cycle of the Ramsay family (1972–1990s): haunted havelis, cursed temples, monster-men and songs, the B-movie strand of Bollywood horror (Purana Mandir, Veerana).

label: Afrofuturist Film
defn: Science fiction of the Afrofuturist movement (the term is Mark Dery's, 1993): Black diasporic and African speculative futures, cosmic myth and technoculture (Space Is the Place, The Brother from Another Planet, Neptune Frost).

label: Bergfilm (Mountain Film)
defn: The German mountain film of the 1920s–30s (Arnold Fanck, Leni Riefenstahl, Luis Trenker): real Alpine climbing and skiing photographed on location, elemental storms and avalanches, romantic rivalry and heroic summits (The Holy Mountain, The White Hell of Pitz Palu, The Blue Light).

label: Lucha Film
defn: The Mexican luchador film (1952–1980s): masked professional wrestlers — El Santo, Blue Demon, Mil Máscaras, the Wrestling Women — fighting vampires, mummies, mad scientists and Martians in action-horror-science-fiction serials (Santo vs. the Vampire Women).

label: Sageuk Film
defn: The Korean historical film (sageuk), set chiefly in the Goryeo and Joseon courts and countryside: palace intrigue, royal doubles, scholars, painters and kisaeng (The King and the Clown, Masquerade, Untold Scandal).

label: Karl May Western
defn: The West German (Rialto/CCC) cycle of 1962–1968 adapting Karl May's Winnetou and Old Shatterhand novels, shot in Yugoslavia: noble Apache chief, German blood-brother hero, Martin Böttcher scores (Treasure of Silver Lake, Apache Gold). It preceded and fed the Spaghetti Western boom.

label: Commedia sexy all'italiana
defn: The Italian erotic comedy cycle of c. 1970–1985: schoolteachers, nurses, policewomen and maids (Edwige Fenech, Gloria Guida, Lino Banfi, Alvaro Vitali) in bawdy, voyeuristic farces descended from the commedia all'italiana and the decamerotici (Malizia, L'insegnante).
see: A12-10 Commedia all'italiana; A12-40 Sex Comedy

label: Carry On Film
defn: The British Carry On series (Peter Rogers and Gerald Thomas, 1958–1978, revived 1992): seaside-postcard innuendo, a stock company (Sid James, Kenneth Williams, Hattie Jacques, Barbara Windsor) and genre and institution parodies (Carry On Nurse, Carry On Up the Khyber).

label: Chanchada
defn: The Brazilian popular musical comedy of the 1930s–1950s, above all Atlântida's carnival films with Oscarito and Grande Otelo: samba numbers, burlesque and parodies of Hollywood (Carnaval Atlântida, Nem Sansão Nem Dalila). Its erotic successor is A15-6 Pornochanchada.

label: Telefoni Bianchi
defn: The Italian sentimental and sophisticated comedies of c. 1932–1943 ('white telephone' films), set among department stores, hotels and Art Deco apartments, after Hollywood and Hungarian models (Mario Camerini, Vittorio De Sica, Mario Soldati): What Scoundrels Men Are!, Il signor Max.

label: Comedia Ranchera
defn: The Mexican ranch musical of the Golden Age (1936–1950s): singing charros (Tito Guízar, Jorge Negrete, Pedro Infante), haciendas, serenades, cockfights and rival suitors (Allá en el Rancho Grande, ¡Ay Jalisco, no te rajes!, Dos tipos de cuidado).
see: A14-12 Rumberas Film; A10-5 Musical Western

label: Huangmei Opera Film
defn: The sung costume romance in Huangmei-opera style, launched in Hong Kong by Li Han-hsiang at Shaw Brothers (1958–1960s) after the mainland Heavenly Match: legendary lovers, cross-dressing heroines, palace and garden sets (The Kingdom and the Beauty, The Love Eterne).

label: Hong Kong Category III Film
defn: A Hong Kong film of the adults-only Category III rating cycle (1988 onward, peaking in the early 1990s): sex-and-violence exploitation, erotic costume romps (Sex and Zen) and lurid true-crime shockers (The Untold Story, Ebola Syndrome). Defined by the named Hong Kong cycle rather than one plot type.
see: A4 Horror; A7-10 Hong Kong Action Cinema

label: Pre-Code Hollywood Film
defn: The Hollywood dramas of c. 1929–1934, between the coming of sound and strict enforcement of the Production Code, that treated sex, adultery, prostitution, crime and Depression misery with a frankness later forbidden (Baby Face, Red-Headed Woman, Heroes for Sale). Pre-Code gangster, horror and musical films stay in their genres.

label: Brat Pack Film
defn: The mid-1980s American youth films starring the 'Brat Pack' (Emilio Estevez, Molly Ringwald, Judd Nelson, Ally Sheedy, Andrew McCarthy, Rob Lowe, Demi Moore, Anthony Michael Hall), above all John Hughes's teen films and Joel Schumacher's post-college ensemble (The Breakfast Club, St. Elmo's Fire).
see: A16-14 Teen Film; A12-37 Teen Comedy

label: Heimatfilm
defn: The German and Austrian homeland film, dominant c. 1947–1960s: Alpine, Black Forest and heath landscapes, foresters, dirndls, folk song and reconciled village communities (Black Forest Girl, Grün ist die Heide), and the critical Neuer or Anti-Heimatfilm of the late 1960s–70s that inverted it.

label: Rubble Film (Trümmerfilm)
defn: The German films of 1946–1949 shot among the bombed ruins, about guilt, returning soldiers, black markets and survival in the immediate post-war (The Murderers Are Among Us, In Those Days).

label: Ozploitation
defn: The Australian low-budget exploitation boom of c. 1971–1990 under the 10BA tax concession: ocker sex comedies, bikie films, outback horror, kung-fu and car-crash action (Stone, Alvin Purple, Patrick, Turkey Shoot, Dead End Drive-In).
see: A1-23 Australian New Wave; A10-10 Meat Pie Western

label: Lettrist & Situationist Cinema
defn: The Paris avant-garde of Isidore Isou's Lettrists (1951–1952) and Guy Debord's Situationist International: 'discrepant' and anti-films that separate sound from image, scratch and blank the film strip, and détourn found images against the spectacle (Venom and Eternity, Howlings in Favour of de Sade, The Society of the Spectacle).
see: A19-4 Essay Film; A20-4 Found-Footage Film
